newsitem.title: UK: N.Irish business leaders cautious on IRA truce.
newsitem.headline: N.Irish business leaders cautious on IRA truce.

text.p: Northern Ireland's business leaders gave a cautious welcome on Monday to news of a ceasefire to the IRA's 28-year war against British rule but said any economic pickup would take time to filter through.

The Northern Ireland Institue of Directors recalled in a statement that the previous Irish Republican Army (IRA) truce in August 1994, which raised high hopes of an economic boom, had collapsed 17 months later.
"The business community has already greeted one ceasefire with increased investment in the province's economy," the Institute said.
"Given subsequent events they wil treat this renewal of the last ceasefire with understandable caution."
The Institute, which groups leading businessmen, said that all-party talks on a lasting political settlement were due to start in September, which "may determine the next 25 years."
"Yesterday's ceasefire may be the most significant 10 months in the history of Northern Ireland," the Institute said.
Accountant Coopers & Lybrand said the economy may take longer than expected to respond to the IRA ceasefire because it faced a "credibility gap" after the previous one broke down.
"That means it may take some time before the economy feels the benefits of any cessation of violence," it said.
"Those who held back in investment before the ceasefire are unlikely to be persuaded to invest until they are convinced that the peace is real," Coopers & Lybrand said.
Managing Partner Stephen Kingon said tourism and the hotel trade would feel the first benefits but other sectors would take longer to react.

"It would be reasonable to expect a measurable improvement in the tourism and hospitality sectors inside the next six months but it has to be remembered that these account for less than three per cent of GDP," he said.
"Given the cautious response to yesterday's announcement, it could be up to two years before the economy picks up as a result of new indigenous and inward investments," it said.
There was no immediate comment from the Industrial Development Board, a state body charged with attracting foreign investment, especially in the hi-tech and computer sectors.

The IDB says foreign investment has reached record levels and that the economy has outperformed the rest of the United Kingdom in many areas because of a robust resistance to the 28-year political and sectarian conflict.
Unemployment hit a 17-year low in June, according to government figures, and manufacturing output growth is outperforming that in England, Scotland and Wales.

The hotel industry said at the weekend that the IRA truce was good news for the image of Northern Ireland but pointed out that many operators had already cancelled tours because of riots earlier this month over Protestant Orange Order parades.
But it said it was now focusing on getting tourists to come to Northern Ireland in the autumn as part of a cross-border plan worked out with the Irish Republic's state tourism body, Bord Failte.
